Paragraph:
Translation: There are the mighty Yudhamanyu, the very powerful Uttamauja, the son of Subhadra and the sons of Draupadi. All these warriors are great chariot fighters.

Purport: [No purport provided for this verse in the source text].
Situation/Problem_Faced: Duryodhana reaches the climax of his anxiety-driven cataloging of the Pandava army's strength, specifically pointing out the elite and powerful 'maharathas' (great chariot fighters) among the younger generation of warriors.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: He continues to project his internal insecurity outward by emphasizing the sheer might and capability of the enemy's allied commanders to his own military chief.
Outcome/Resolution: This exhaustive listing serves to fully articulate Duryodhana's threat perception, establishing the formidable nature of the opposition in his own mind and Dronacarya's.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Bhaya (Overwhelming fear arising from materialistic attachment and unrighteous actions)
Ahamkara (The ego's tendency to feel threatened and shrink when faced with righteous opposition)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The verse concludes Duryodhana's assessment of the opposing forces. Spiritually, it highlights the exhaustion of the materialistic mind, which is perpetually restless and insecure because it places its faith entirely in worldly power and numerical strength rather than divine truth or dharma.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Duryodhana's psychological state is characterized by profound threat magnification and hyper-arousal. By detailing even the sons of his enemies as 'great chariot fighters,' he reveals a pervasive anxiety that leaves no room for confidence, demonstrating how guilt and moral compromise inherently weaken psychological resilience.
